** Role Overview

This is a *Fractional CTO & Engagement Director* role — a dual mandate that combines
senior technical leadership with client engagement accountability. It is the single
point of authority between Yamaha Music Innovation Fund and all of Sedin's internal
units, operating across three layers simultaneously:

- *Technical:* Own the technology vision, architecture decisions, and engineering
  standards across everything being built for Yamaha
- *External:* Be the face, voice, and conscience of the entire engagement for Yamaha
- *Internal:* Force coherence across Code Rapper, Data Culture, Marketing, and
  Tarka Labs before anything touches the client

The existential risk: Yamaha sees four vendors in a trenchcoat with no shared
technical direction. The win condition: they see one high-trust partner who can
make the right technology call and deliver it.

*Industry equivalents:*
- *Fractional CTO (technical layer):* The on-demand CTO model used by Pilot, Toptal,
  and YC-backed firms for early-stage and mid-size companies that need senior
  technical leadership without a full-time hire. The Fractional CTO owns strategy,
  architecture, standards, and vendor decisions — not day-to-day coding.
- *Engagement Director (client layer):* Client Partner at Accenture or ThoughtWorks,
  Engagement Director at Deloitte. Accountable for the relationship, delivery, and
  commercial outcomes. Carries a growth mandate alongside the delivery mandate.

Together, this role gives Yamaha what most consulting engagements lack: a single
person who can speak both the language of technology decisions and the language of
business outcomes.

** Immediate Priorities: The June Deadline
:PROPERTIES:
:CATEGORY: Yamaha
:END:

Yamaha needs to see value by end of June. Billing unlocks only after this. Everything
else is secondary to this milestone.

*** TODO Define what "value" means to Yamaha — in writing
DEADLINE: <2026-06-06 Fri>
:PROPERTIES:
:CONTEXT:  Ask Yamaha's 4-person team directly and asynchronously
:END:
Do they want a live Creator Pass milestone? A data dashboard? A roadmap presentation?
A benchmark vs. competitors? Get the definition in writing so delivery targets the
right thing, not our interpretation of it.

*** TODO Stakeholder map: identify who at Yamaha decides, influences, and blocks
DEADLINE: <2026-06-06 Fri>
:PROPERTIES:
:CONTEXT:  The 4-person YMIF team is not flat
:END:
Map each person's role, priorities, and what success looks like to them personally.
Know this before the June value review — presenting to the wrong priority is a miss
even if the delivery is strong.

*** TODO Map all shippable / demonstrable deliverables across internal teams by June 30
DEADLINE: <2026-06-02 Mon>
Survey Code Rapper, Data Culture, Marketing, and Tarka Labs. What is done or
near-done? What can be polished for a client-facing demo in 4 weeks?

*** TODO Pick 1-2 flagship deliverables for the end-of-June showcase
DEADLINE: <2026-06-06 Fri>
Do not try to show everything. Sequence the most impressive 1-2 things front and
center. Everything else is supporting context.

*** TODO Create and distribute the June Delivery Brief (1 page, internal)
DEADLINE: <2026-06-06 Fri>
One shared document. All four teams aligned to the same finish line. Include:
what we're showcasing, who owns what, the narrative we're telling Yamaha.

*** TODO Prepare the end-of-June value presentation (Yamaha-facing)
DEADLINE: <2026-06-20 Sat>
One deck, one voice, one team. Bring one strategic recommendation they didn't ask
for. Review internally before sending anything to Yamaha.

** Daily Operating Rhythm

*** Morning (30 min)

| Activity                                         | Purpose                                     |
|--------------------------------------------------+---------------------------------------------|
| Scan all Yamaha threads / email                  | Nothing surprises you in client calls       |
| Attend or review dept. standups; note key points | Know blockers before they fester — =C-c c ys= |
| Identify the one thing that could go wrong today | Fix it before it becomes a client issue     |
| Check delivery tracker for overdue items         | No commitment falls through the cracks      |

*** Core Day

*Internal — keep short, keep tight:*
- Attend dept. standups; you summarise the key points (what shipped, what's next,
  any blockers) — no extra work pushed onto leads. Capture with =C-c c ys=.
- Synthesize into one coherent picture before any client interaction
- Escalate blockers before EOD, not tomorrow
- Update the risk register if anything material shifts

*External — deliberate, controlled:*
- All Yamaha communication routes through you
- If another team member communicates directly, you are CC'd and pre-approved
- Respond to Yamaha within 2 hours during business hours — speed signals confidence
- Bring one proactive observation or idea per week — don't just report status

*** End of Day (15 min)

- Update the delivery tracker
- Flag any Yamaha ask without an assigned owner
- Send a proactive note to Yamaha if something meaningful shipped — don't wait for
  the weekly call

** Weekly Rhythm

| Day       | Activities                                                                               |
|-----------+------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Monday    | 1. Internal sync with all dept. leads — commitments vs. reality gap. (=C-c c yi=)        |
|           | 2. Update risk register — new risks? mitigations to action? (=C-c c yr=)                 |
| Tuesday   | Account growth review — any expansion opportunity to surface this week?                  |
| Wednesday | Written status update to Yamaha (3-5 bullets: shipped, next, decisions needed from them) |
| Thursday  | Architecture & technical review — decisions made this week, anything to challenge?       |
|           | Review stakeholder map — any new contacts, any relationship that needs warming?          |
| Friday    | 1. Yamaha call or async Loom — you present, one voice. (=C-c c ym=)                      |
|           | 2. Internal retro — what comms went sideways, what coordination failed, fix it           |

** Monthly and Quarterly Rhythms

These cadences are standard in engagement director and client partner roles and are
typically absent from informal consulting arrangements. They are what separates a
vendor relationship from a strategic partnership.

*** Monthly: Client Health Check
- Send Yamaha a brief satisfaction pulse — 3 questions max, async format
- Qualitative: what's working, what would they change, what would they love to see
- Review internally and identify one thing to improve and one to double down on
- Do not wait for problems to surface organically

*** Monthly: Commercial Review
- Track billable time vs. SOW commitments
- Flag scope creep within 48 hours of identifying it — bring it to Yamaha as an
  opportunity, not a dispute: "here's what we can add and what it would take"
- Ensure invoices are sent on time and match the SOW exactly — late or inaccurate
  invoices erode trust faster than delivery misses
- Identify any expansion of work that should be covered by a new or amended SOW

*** Quarterly: Executive Business Review (QBR)
- 60-90 minute structured session with Yamaha senior stakeholders
- Cover: what we delivered, business impact achieved, what's next, roadmap alignment
- Bring one strategic recommendation they didn't ask for — this is the "trusted
  advisor" signal
- Document outcomes and send a written summary within 24 hours of the call
- Use QBR to surface the renewal or expansion conversation naturally

** Communication Framework

*** The Cardinal Rule

Yamaha should never see the seams between Sedin departments.

- One Slack channel or email thread with Yamaha, owned by you
- Departments do not CC Yamaha on inter-team coordination
- Disagreements are resolved internally before Yamaha hears anything
- All commitments to Yamaha are made by you — only you commit timelines and scope

*** The "One Team" Narrative

In every Yamaha touchpoint:
- Use "we" — not "our Tarka Labs team" or "our data team"
- Reference capabilities, not org structure: "we have deep expertise in X"
- Prepare a one-paragraph team introduction for any new Yamaha stakeholder that
  frames the team as a single integrated unit

*** Escalation Protocol

If a department will miss a commitment:
1. You find out as early as possible (the daily standup habit is what enables this)
2. You tell Yamaha *before* the deadline, *not after*, with a revised plan in hand
3. You own the message — never "our marketing team dropped the ball"

Log any commitment (made or received) immediately with =C-c c yc=.

*** Communication Templates to Build

- [ ] Weekly status update (consistent format, 3-5 bullets, takes 10 min to write)
- [ ] Escalation notice (acknowledge, explain, revised plan — no blame)
- [ ] New stakeholder introduction (one paragraph, one-team narrative)
- [ ] Meeting follow-up / action items (sent within 2 hours of any call)
- [ ] Scope change framing (opportunity framing, not dispute framing)

** Internal Coordination Model

*** Department Lead Relationships

Treat each lead as your delivery partner for their domain. Establish with each:
- Weekly 30-min 1:1
- A shared tracker they update (not a meeting — a doc)
- Clear ownership split: they own *how*, you own *what and when* with the client

The four leads to align:
1. Code Rapper — development / technical delivery
2. Data Culture — data, analytics, insights workstream
3. Marketing — brand, content, client-facing materials
4. Tarka Labs — engineering / product leadership

*** Yamaha Engagement Overview (Internal Brief)

A single document every team member reads before touching this account:
- What we've committed to and by when
- Who owns each workstream by department
- Yamaha's success criteria (in their words, not ours)
- Key contacts at Yamaha: names, roles, what success looks like to each of them
- What we must *not* say or surface externally: internal tensions, org structure,
  billing disputes, staffing issues, cross-department friction

Every new person touching this engagement reads this brief before their first
client email or call.

*** New Team Member Onboarding Protocol

Standard practice in enterprise consulting; typically missing in agency engagements.
- *Brief:* Read the Yamaha Engagement Overview before first client contact
- *Shadow:* Sit in on at least one client call before speaking in one
- *Introduction:* You introduce them to Yamaha, with context on their role and
  what capability they bring to the team

*** Preventing the "Many Vendors" Problem

- One slide deck template for all Yamaha presentations
- One tone of voice: professional, capable, collaborative, commercially aware
- One project board / tracker that all teams update — Yamaha can have read access
- No department-specific branding in client deliverables

** Delivery Management

*** Delivery Tracker

A living document updated daily, reviewed weekly. Add new entries with =C-c c yc=.

| Commitment            | Made On | Promised By | Owner (internal) | Status      | Yamaha Notified? |
|-----------------------+---------+-------------+------------------+-------------+------------------|
| Creator Pass checkout | May 12  | May 19      | Tarka Labs       | Done        | Yes              |
| [next item]           |         |             |                  | In Progress |                  |

Any row where "Owner" is blank is a fire. Any row where "Yamaha Notified?" is No
and Status is Done is a missed opportunity.

*** Risk Register

Standard in Engagement Director and Program Director roles; typically absent from
informal consulting arrangements. Review in Monday's internal sync. Log new risks
as they surface with =C-c c yr=.

| Risk                              | Likelihood | Impact | Mitigation                                   | Owner       |
|-----------------------------------+------------+--------+----------------------------------------------+-------------|
| Internal coordination breakdown   | High       | High   | Daily async standup, weekly sync, you as hub  | You         |
| Scope creep without billing       | Medium     | High   | SOW review monthly, 48hr escalation rule      | You         |
| Key person dependency at Yamaha   | Medium     | Medium | Build relationships with 2+ contacts          | You         |
| Delivery miss at end of June      | Medium     | High   | Weekly tracker, buffer built into estimates   | Dept. leads |
| Yamaha loses confidence in unity  | Low        | High   | Consistent comms discipline, one-voice rule   | You         |
| New stakeholder without briefing  | Low        | Medium | Onboarding protocol, read brief before call   | You         |

*** Scope and Commercial Management

- Maintain an active log of scope changes and decisions
- Flag any out-of-scope work within 48 hours of identifying it
- Frame additions as opportunities: "here's what we can add and what it would take"
- Review SOW monthly — know exactly what is and isn't covered
- Ensure invoices are sent on time and reconcile against the delivery tracker

** Account Growth and Strategy

This is a forward-looking dimension standard in Client Partner roles. It distinguishes
a vendor (delivers what's asked) from a strategic partner (shapes what gets asked).

*** Know Their Roadmap

- Understand what YMIF is building for the next 12 months beyond Creator Pass
- Identify where Sedin could play before Yamaha has to ask
- Bring one strategic recommendation per quarter that they didn't ask for

*** Expansion Opportunities Within the Account

#+begin_example
Creator Pass v2        — Features beyond the current Shopify build
Data & Analytics       — 10M customer base is an asset; what can be done with it?
AI/ML in Music         — Adjacent to the YMIF portfolio investment thesis
Other Portfolio Cos    — YMIF invests in startups; other portfolio companies may
                         need the same technology partnership
#+end_example

*** Business Context: Know Their Business, Not Just the Project

Standard at Accenture/ThoughtWorks: every person on a client engagement should
be able to answer:
- What business outcome does Creator Pass ultimately serve for Yamaha?
- What would make this project fail, and have we named that risk explicitly?
- What would we recommend if we were Yamaha's CTO?

Embed this in every project kickoff: 30 min on client business context, not just
technical context.

*** Competitive Awareness

- Know who else Yamaha is evaluating or working with
- Know what they are trying to build internally vs. outsource
- Keep the "2-3 months vs. 8 months" delivery advantage visible — it is the
  strongest proof point we have

** Proving the Model: The Replication Playbook

The meta-objective: prove that Sedin can operate as a unified technology partner at
the $1M+ level, then repeat the model for other accounts.

- Keep a running engagement log: what worked, what failed, what surprised
- After June (billing unlocked), write a one-page internal case study:
  - How we delivered
  - What the client valued most
  - What the internal coordination model looked like
  - What we'd do differently
- This becomes the *Sedin Unified Partner Playbook* — the template for the next
  Yamaha-type client

** Success Metrics

| Timeframe   | What Success Looks Like                                              |
|-------------+----------------------------------------------------------------------|
| End of June | Yamaha sees the value demo and billing unlocks                       |
| End of June | Zero client-visible coordination failures or "many teams" moments    |

| Q3          | At least one expansion opportunity identified and in discussion       |
| Q3          | Yamaha is not comparing us to what they could build internally        |
| Q4          | Engagement cited as proof case for Sedin unified partner model       |
| Long term   | Yamaha is a $1M+ annually renewable account                          |

** The Single Most Important Habit

Know what Yamaha is thinking *before* they say it. Proactive communication beats
reactive firefighting every time. The best client partners in the industry spend
more time thinking about the client's next problem than their own next deliverable.

* Yamaha Engagement: Role Plan
:PROPERTIES:
:CATEGORY: Yamaha
:END:

** Role Overview

This is a *Fractional CTO & Engagement Director* role — a dual mandate that combines
senior technical leadership with client engagement accountability. It is the single
point of authority between Yamaha Music Innovation Fund and all of Sedin's internal
units, operating across three layers simultaneously:

- *Technical:* Own the technology vision, architecture decisions, and engineering
  standards across everything being built for Yamaha
- *External:* Be the face, voice, and conscience of the entire engagement for Yamaha
- *Internal:* Force coherence across Code Rapper, Data Culture, Marketing, and
  Tarka Labs before anything touches the client

The existential risk: Yamaha sees four vendors in a trenchcoat with no shared
technical direction. The win condition: they see one high-trust partner who can
make the right technology call and deliver it.

*Industry equivalents:*
- *Fractional CTO (technical layer):* The on-demand CTO model used by Pilot, Toptal,
  and YC-backed firms for early-stage and mid-size companies that need senior
  technical leadership without a full-time hire. The Fractional CTO owns strategy,
  architecture, standards, and vendor decisions — not day-to-day coding.
- *Engagement Director (client layer):* Client Partner at Accenture or ThoughtWorks,
  Engagement Director at Deloitte. Accountable for the relationship, delivery, and
  commercial outcomes. Carries a growth mandate alongside the delivery mandate.

Together, this role gives Yamaha what most consulting engagements lack: a single
person who can speak both the language of technology decisions and the language of
business outcomes.

** Immediate Priorities: The June Deadline
:PROPERTIES:
:CATEGORY: Yamaha
:END:

Yamaha needs to see value by end of June. Billing unlocks only after this. Everything
else is secondary to this milestone.

** Daily Operating Rhythm

*** Morning (30 min)

| Activity                                         | Purpose                                     |
|--------------------------------------------------+---------------------------------------------|
| Scan all Yamaha threads / email                  | Nothing surprises you in client calls       |
| Attend or review dept. standups; note key points | Know blockers before they fester — =C-c c ys= |
| Identify the one thing that could go wrong today | Fix it before it becomes a client issue     |
| Check delivery tracker for overdue items         | No commitment falls through the cracks      |

*** Core Day

*Internal — keep short, keep tight:*
- Attend dept. standups; you summarise the key points (what shipped, what's next,
  any blockers) — no extra work pushed onto leads. Capture with =C-c c ys=.
- Synthesize into one coherent picture before any client interaction
- Escalate blockers before EOD, not tomorrow
- Update the risk register if anything material shifts

*External — deliberate, controlled:*
- All Yamaha communication routes through you
- If another team member communicates directly, you are CC'd and pre-approved
- Respond to Yamaha within 2 hours during business hours — speed signals confidence
- Bring one proactive observation or idea per week — don't just report status

*** End of Day (15 min)

- Update the delivery tracker
- Flag any Yamaha ask without an assigned owner
- Send a proactive note to Yamaha if something meaningful shipped — don't wait for
  the weekly call

** Weekly Rhythm

| Day       | Activities                                                                               |
|-----------+------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Monday    | 1. Internal sync with all dept. leads — commitments vs. reality gap. (=C-c c yi=)        |
|           | 2. Update risk register — new risks? mitigations to action? (=C-c c yr=)                 |
| Tuesday   | Account growth review — any expansion opportunity to surface this week?                  |
| Wednesday | Written status update to Yamaha (3-5 bullets: shipped, next, decisions needed from them) |
| Thursday  | Architecture & technical review — decisions made this week, anything to challenge?       |
|           | Review stakeholder map — any new contacts, any relationship that needs warming?          |
| Friday    | 1. Yamaha call or async Loom — you present, one voice. (=C-c c ym=)                      |
|           | 2. Internal retro — what comms went sideways, what coordination failed, fix it           |

** Monthly and Quarterly Rhythms

These cadences are standard in engagement director and client partner roles and are
typically absent from informal consulting arrangements. They are what separates a
vendor relationship from a strategic partnership.

*** Monthly: Client Health Check
- Send Yamaha a brief satisfaction pulse — 3 questions max, async format
- Qualitative: what's working, what would they change, what would they love to see
- Review internally and identify one thing to improve and one to double down on
- Do not wait for problems to surface organically

*** Monthly: Commercial Review
- Track billable time vs. SOW commitments
- Flag scope creep within 48 hours of identifying it — bring it to Yamaha as an
  opportunity, not a dispute: "here's what we can add and what it would take"
- Ensure invoices are sent on time and match the SOW exactly — late or inaccurate
  invoices erode trust faster than delivery misses
- Identify any expansion of work that should be covered by a new or amended SOW

*** Quarterly: Executive Business Review (QBR)
- 60-90 minute structured session with Yamaha senior stakeholders
- Cover: what we delivered, business impact achieved, what's next, roadmap alignment
- Bring one strategic recommendation they didn't ask for — this is the "trusted
  advisor" signal
- Document outcomes and send a written summary within 24 hours of the call
- Use QBR to surface the renewal or expansion conversation naturally

** Communication Framework

*** The Cardinal Rule

Yamaha should never see the seams between Sedin departments.

- One Slack channel or email thread with Yamaha, owned by you
- Departments do not CC Yamaha on inter-team coordination
- Disagreements are resolved internally before Yamaha hears anything
- All commitments to Yamaha are made by you — only you commit timelines and scope

*** The "One Team" Narrative

In every Yamaha touchpoint:
- Use "we" — not "our Tarka Labs team" or "our data team"
- Reference capabilities, not org structure: "we have deep expertise in X"
- Prepare a one-paragraph team introduction for any new Yamaha stakeholder that
  frames the team as a single integrated unit

*** Escalation Protocol

If a department will miss a commitment:
1. You find out as early as possible (the daily standup habit is what enables this)
2. You tell Yamaha *before* the deadline, *not after*, with a revised plan in hand
3. You own the message — never "our marketing team dropped the ball"

Log any commitment (made or received) immediately with =C-c c yc=.

*** Communication Templates to Build

- [ ] Weekly status update (consistent format, 3-5 bullets, takes 10 min to write)
- [ ] Escalation notice (acknowledge, explain, revised plan — no blame)
- [ ] New stakeholder introduction (one paragraph, one-team narrative)
- [ ] Meeting follow-up / action items (sent within 2 hours of any call)
- [ ] Scope change framing (opportunity framing, not dispute framing)

** Internal Coordination Model

*** Department Lead Relationships

Treat each lead as your delivery partner for their domain. Establish with each:
- Weekly 30-min 1:1
- A shared tracker they update (not a meeting — a doc)
- Clear ownership split: they own *how*, you own *what and when* with the client

The four leads to align:
1. Code Rapper — development / technical delivery
2. Data Culture — data, analytics, insights workstream
3. Marketing — brand, content, client-facing materials
4. Tarka Labs — engineering / product leadership

*** Yamaha Engagement Overview (Internal Brief)

A single document every team member reads before touching this account:
- What we've committed to and by when
- Who owns each workstream by department
- Yamaha's success criteria (in their words, not ours)
- Key contacts at Yamaha: names, roles, what success looks like to each of them
- What we must *not* say or surface externally: internal tensions, org structure,
  billing disputes, staffing issues, cross-department friction

Every new person touching this engagement reads this brief before their first
client email or call.

*** New Team Member Onboarding Protocol

Standard practice in enterprise consulting; typically missing in agency engagements.
- *Brief:* Read the Yamaha Engagement Overview before first client contact
- *Shadow:* Sit in on at least one client call before speaking in one
- *Introduction:* You introduce them to Yamaha, with context on their role and
  what capability they bring to the team

*** Preventing the "Many Vendors" Problem

- One slide deck template for all Yamaha presentations
- One tone of voice: professional, capable, collaborative, commercially aware
- One project board / tracker that all teams update — Yamaha can have read access
- No department-specific branding in client deliverables

** Delivery Management

*** Delivery Tracker

A living document updated daily, reviewed weekly. Add new entries with =C-c c yc=.

| Commitment            | Made On | Promised By | Owner (internal) | Status      | Yamaha Notified? |
|-----------------------+---------+-------------+------------------+-------------+------------------|
| Creator Pass checkout | May 12  | May 19      | Tarka Labs       | Done        | Yes              |
| [next item]           |         |             |                  | In Progress |                  |

Any row where "Owner" is blank is a fire. Any row where "Yamaha Notified?" is No
and Status is Done is a missed opportunity.

*** Risk Register

Standard in Engagement Director and Program Director roles; typically absent from
informal consulting arrangements. Review in Monday's internal sync. Log new risks
as they surface with =C-c c yr=.

| Risk                              | Likelihood | Impact | Mitigation                                   | Owner       |
|-----------------------------------+------------+--------+----------------------------------------------+-------------|
| Internal coordination breakdown   | High       | High   | Daily async standup, weekly sync, you as hub  | You         |
| Scope creep without billing       | Medium     | High   | SOW review monthly, 48hr escalation rule      | You         |
| Key person dependency at Yamaha   | Medium     | Medium | Build relationships with 2+ contacts          | You         |
| Delivery miss at end of June      | Medium     | High   | Weekly tracker, buffer built into estimates   | Dept. leads |
| Yamaha loses confidence in unity  | Low        | High   | Consistent comms discipline, one-voice rule   | You         |
| New stakeholder without briefing  | Low        | Medium | Onboarding protocol, read brief before call   | You         |

*** Scope and Commercial Management

- Maintain an active log of scope changes and decisions
- Flag any out-of-scope work within 48 hours of identifying it
- Frame additions as opportunities: "here's what we can add and what it would take"
- Review SOW monthly — know exactly what is and isn't covered
- Ensure invoices are sent on time and reconcile against the delivery tracker

** Account Growth and Strategy

This is a forward-looking dimension standard in Client Partner roles. It distinguishes
a vendor (delivers what's asked) from a strategic partner (shapes what gets asked).

*** Know Their Roadmap

- Understand what YMIF is building for the next 12 months beyond Creator Pass
- Identify where Sedin could play before Yamaha has to ask
- Bring one strategic recommendation per quarter that they didn't ask for

*** Expansion Opportunities Within the Account

#+begin_example
Creator Pass v2        — Features beyond the current Shopify build
Data & Analytics       — 10M customer base is an asset; what can be done with it?
AI/ML in Music         — Adjacent to the YMIF portfolio investment thesis
Other Portfolio Cos    — YMIF invests in startups; other portfolio companies may
                         need the same technology partnership
#+end_example

*** Business Context: Know Their Business, Not Just the Project

Standard at Accenture/ThoughtWorks: every person on a client engagement should
be able to answer:
- What business outcome does Creator Pass ultimately serve for Yamaha?
- What would make this project fail, and have we named that risk explicitly?
- What would we recommend if we were Yamaha's CTO?

Embed this in every project kickoff: 30 min on client business context, not just
technical context.

*** Competitive Awareness

- Know who else Yamaha is evaluating or working with
- Know what they are trying to build internally vs. outsource
- Keep the "2-3 months vs. 8 months" delivery advantage visible — it is the
  strongest proof point we have

** Technical Architecture & Fractional CTO Responsibilities

This section covers the technical leadership mandate — distinct from the engagement
and delivery dimensions above. As Fractional CTO, the remit is to own the technology
direction for Yamaha, not to execute it day-to-day.

*** Technical Strategy & Roadmap

- Maintain a living technology roadmap for Yamaha — not just what's being built now,
  but where the platform needs to go in 6-18 months
- Current platform (Shopify + custom integrations) is a GTM vehicle, not a long-term
  architecture; own the decision of when and how to evolve beyond it
- Define the data strategy for the 10M Yamaha customer base — the platform is
  sitting on a significant data asset that is currently underutilised
- Align the technology roadmap to YMIF's investment thesis (music startups, AI in
  music) — identify where technology decisions open or close future options

*** Architecture Oversight

- Review and approve all significant architectural decisions across teams — Code
  Rapper, Data Culture, and Tarka Labs should not make major technology choices
  without your sign-off
- Ensure architectural coherence across the six separate product areas (Spotify
  integration, AI features, etc.) — fragmentation here is a long-term liability
- Maintain a set of Architecture Decision Records (ADRs) for key choices made —
  rationale, alternatives considered, trade-offs accepted
- Conduct a quarterly architecture health review: scalability, maintainability,
  integration fragility, dependency risk

*** Build vs. Buy Advisory

Every significant technology decision should go through this lens before commitment:
- *Build:* When it is core to Yamaha's competitive differentiation
- *Buy:* When a proven SaaS/API solution covers 80%+ of the need
- *Partner:* When the capability is better sourced from a specialist

Current areas requiring a clear build/buy position:
- Creator Pass payment and subscription infrastructure (beyond Shopify's defaults)
- Music metadata and rights management
- AI/ML capabilities for music recommendations or creation tools
- Analytics and data warehouse for customer insights

*** Technical Due Diligence

Regular reviews of what has been built — not to micromanage, but to catch problems
before they become client-visible crises:
- *Monthly:* Code quality spot-check across active workstreams — not a full audit,
  a targeted review of the highest-risk areas
- *Quarterly:* Full technical health review covering security posture, performance
  benchmarks, test coverage, and documentation completeness
- *On handoff:* Any work delivered by a new team or vendor gets a technical review
  before it is presented to Yamaha as done

*** Security & Compliance

Creator Pass is a consumer platform touching payment data and personal information
at scale. This cannot be treated as a delivery team concern — it is a CTO concern.

*Immediate posture to establish:*
- Payment flow: PCI DSS compliance scope — know what Shopify covers and what falls
  on the application layer
- Data privacy: GDPR and CCPA obligations for the 10M customer base — consent,
  data retention, right to deletion
- API security: authentication, rate limiting, and input validation across all
  custom integrations
- Third-party vendor risk: any SaaS tool that touches customer data needs to be
  assessed for data handling practices

*Ongoing:*
- Security is a standing agenda item in the monthly commercial review
- Any new integration or vendor must pass a lightweight security checklist before
  approval
- Incident response plan: define what happens if there is a data breach or outage

*** Vendor & Technology Evaluation

Yamaha should not commit to any significant technology vendor or tool without your
input. Establish a lightweight evaluation process:
1. What problem does this solve, and is there a better alternative?
2. What does lock-in look like, and is it acceptable?
3. What are the data handling and security practices?
4. What is the total cost of ownership over 2 years, not just the licence fee?
5. Can we exit cleanly if needed?

Maintain a vendor register: what tools are in use, what they touch, renewal dates,
and any known risks.

*** Engineering Standards

Set the quality bar across all teams working on this account:
- *Definition of Done:* A feature is not done until it is tested, documented, and
  reviewed. Agree this with all four department leads and hold to it.
- *Code review:* All production code gets reviewed before merge — no exceptions for
  deadline pressure
- *Documentation:* Every integration, API, and non-obvious architectural decision
  gets documented. The knowledge must not live only in engineers' heads.
- *Incident response:* Production incidents get a brief post-mortem (5 mins written)
  — not to assign blame, but to prevent recurrence

*** Team & Hiring Advisory

As Fractional CTO, you have a view across both Sedin's team and Yamaha's internal
capability. Use it:
- Assess whether the current team mix (Code Rapper, Data Culture, Marketing, Tarka
  Labs) has the right skills for where the platform needs to go in 12 months
- Advise Yamaha on any internal technical hires they are considering — role design,
  interview approach, what to look for
- Flag skill gaps before they become delivery risks: if no one on the team has built
  at the scale Creator Pass needs, say so early

*** Innovation Pipeline

A Fractional CTO is not just a technical guardian — they are a source of technical
opportunity. Bring one relevant technology idea per quarter that Yamaha didn't ask
for:
- AI/ML applications specific to music (recommendation, generation, rights detection)
- Data monetisation opportunities from the 10M customer base
- Emerging platforms or protocols relevant to the music industry
- Technical patterns from YMIF's portfolio companies that could benefit Creator Pass

Frame these as business opportunities first, technology solutions second.

** Proving the Model: The Replication Playbook

The meta-objective: prove that Sedin can operate as a unified technology partner at
the $1M+ level, then repeat the model for other accounts.

- Keep a running engagement log: what worked, what failed, what surprised
- After June (billing unlocked), write a one-page internal case study:
  - How we delivered
  - What the client valued most
  - What the internal coordination model looked like
  - What we'd do differently
- This becomes the *Sedin Unified Partner Playbook* — the template for the next
  Yamaha-type client

** Success Metrics

| Timeframe   | What Success Looks Like                                              |
|-------------+----------------------------------------------------------------------|
| End of June | Yamaha sees the value demo and billing unlocks                       |
| End of June | Zero client-visible coordination failures or "many teams" moments    |
| End of June | Yamaha knows your name and asks for you specifically                 |
| Q3          | At least one expansion opportunity identified and in discussion       |
| Q3          | Yamaha is not comparing us to what they could build internally        |
| Q4          | Engagement cited as proof case for Sedin unified partner model       |
| Long term   | Yamaha is a $1M+ annually renewable account                          |

** The Single Most Important Habit

Know what Yamaha is thinking *before* they say it. Proactive communication beats
reactive firefighting every time. The best client partners in the industry spend
more time thinking about the client's next problem than their own next deliverable.

:CATEGORY: Yamaha

** Role Overview

This is a *Fractional CTO & Engagement Director* role — a dual mandate that combines
senior technical leadership with client engagement accountability. It is the single
point of authority between Yamaha Music Innovation Fund and all of Sedin's internal
units, operating across three layers simultaneously:

- *Technical:* Own the technology vision, architecture decisions, and engineering
  standards across everything being built for Yamaha
- *External:* Be the face, voice, and conscience of the entire engagement for Yamaha
- *Internal:* Force coherence across Code Rapper, Data Culture, Marketing, and
  Tarka Labs before anything touches the client

The existential risk: Yamaha sees four vendors in a trenchcoat with no shared
technical direction. The win condition: they see one high-trust partner who can
make the right technology call and deliver it.

*Industry equivalents:*
- *Fractional CTO (technical layer):* The on-demand CTO model used by Pilot, Toptal,
  and YC-backed firms for early-stage and mid-size companies that need senior
  technical leadership without a full-time hire. The Fractional CTO owns strategy,
  architecture, standards, and vendor decisions — not day-to-day coding.
- *Engagement Director (client layer):* Client Partner at Accenture or ThoughtWorks,
  Engagement Director at Deloitte. Accountable for the relationship, delivery, and
  commercial outcomes. Carries a growth mandate alongside the delivery mandate.

Together, this role gives Yamaha what most consulting engagements lack: a single
person who can speak both the language of technology decisions and the language of
business outcomes.

** Monthly and Quarterly Rhythms

These cadences are standard in engagement director and client partner roles and are
typically absent from informal consulting arrangements. They are what separates a
vendor relationship from a strategic partnership.

*** Monthly: Client Health Check
- Send Yamaha a brief satisfaction pulse — 3 questions max, async format
- Qualitative: what's working, what would they change, what would they love to see
- Review internally and identify one thing to improve and one to double down on
- Do not wait for problems to surface organically

*** Monthly: Commercial Review
- Track billable time vs. SOW commitments
- Flag scope creep within 48 hours of identifying it — bring it to Yamaha as an
  opportunity, not a dispute: "here's what we can add and what it would take"
- Ensure invoices are sent on time and match the SOW exactly — late or inaccurate
  invoices erode trust faster than delivery misses
- Identify any expansion of work that should be covered by a new or amended SOW

*** Quarterly: Executive Business Review (QBR)
- 60-90 minute structured session with Yamaha senior stakeholders
- Cover: what we delivered, business impact achieved, what's next, roadmap alignment
- Bring one strategic recommendation they didn't ask for — this is the "trusted
  advisor" signal
- Document outcomes and send a written summary within 24 hours of the call
- Use QBR to surface the renewal or expansion conversation naturally

** Communication Framework

*** The Cardinal Rule

Yamaha should never see the seams between Sedin departments.

- One Slack channel or email thread with Yamaha, owned by you
- Departments do not CC Yamaha on inter-team coordination
- Disagreements are resolved internally before Yamaha hears anything
- All commitments to Yamaha are made by you — only you commit timelines and scope

*** The "One Team" Narrative

In every Yamaha touchpoint:
- Use "we" — not "our Tarka Labs team" or "our data team"
- Reference capabilities, not org structure: "we have deep expertise in X"
- Prepare a one-paragraph team introduction for any new Yamaha stakeholder that
  frames the team as a single integrated unit

*** Escalation Protocol

If a department will miss a commitment:
1. You find out as early as possible (the daily standup habit is what enables this)
2. You tell Yamaha *before* the deadline, *not after*, with a revised plan in hand
3. You own the message — never "our marketing team dropped the ball"

Log any commitment (made or received) immediately with =C-c c yc=.

*** Communication Templates to Build

- [ ] Weekly status update (consistent format, 3-5 bullets, takes 10 min to write)
- [ ] Escalation notice (acknowledge, explain, revised plan — no blame)
- [ ] New stakeholder introduction (one paragraph, one-team narrative)
- [ ] Meeting follow-up / action items (sent within 2 hours of any call)
- [ ] Scope change framing (opportunity framing, not dispute framing)

** Internal Coordination Model

*** Department Lead Relationships

Treat each lead as your delivery partner for their domain. Establish with each:
- Weekly 30-min 1:1
- A shared tracker they update (not a meeting — a doc)
- Clear ownership split: they own *how*, you own *what and when* with the client

The four leads to align:
1. Code Rapper — development / technical delivery
2. Data Culture — data, analytics, insights workstream
3. Marketing — brand, content, client-facing materials
4. Tarka Labs — engineering / product leadership

*** Yamaha Engagement Overview (Internal Brief)

A single document every team member reads before touching this account:
- What we've committed to and by when
- Who owns each workstream by department
- Yamaha's success criteria (in their words, not ours)
- Key contacts at Yamaha: names, roles, what success looks like to each of them
- What we must *not* say or surface externally: internal tensions, org structure,
  billing disputes, staffing issues, cross-department friction

Every new person touching this engagement reads this brief before their first
client email or call.

*** New Team Member Onboarding Protocol

Standard practice in enterprise consulting; typically missing in agency engagements.
- *Brief:* Read the Yamaha Engagement Overview before first client contact
- *Shadow:* Sit in on at least one client call before speaking in one
- *Introduction:* You introduce them to Yamaha, with context on their role and
  what capability they bring to the team

*** Preventing the "Many Vendors" Problem

- One slide deck template for all Yamaha presentations
- One tone of voice: professional, capable, collaborative, commercially aware
- One project board / tracker that all teams update — Yamaha can have read access
- No department-specific branding in client deliverables

*** Scope and Commercial Management

- Ensure invoices are sent on time and reconcile against the delivery tracker

** Account Growth and Strategy

This is a forward-looking dimension standard in Client Partner roles. It distinguishes
a vendor (delivers what's asked) from a strategic partner (shapes what gets asked).

*** Know Their Roadmap

- Understand what YMIF is building for the next 12 months beyond Creator Pass
- Identify where Sedin could play before Yamaha has to ask
- Bring one strategic recommendation per quarter that they didn't ask for

*** Expansion Opportunities Within the Account

Creator Pass v2        — Features beyond the current Shopify build

AI/ML in Music         — Adjacent to the YMIF portfolio investment thesis

                         need the same technology partnership
#+end_example

*** Business Context: Know Their Business, Not Just the Project

Standard at Accenture/ThoughtWorks: every person on a client engagement should
be able to answer:
- What business outcome does Creator Pass ultimately serve for Yamaha?
- What would make this project fail, and have we named that risk explicitly?
- What would we recommend if we were Yamaha's CTO?

Embed this in every project kickoff: 30 min on client business context, not just
technical context.

*** Competitive Awareness

- Know who else Yamaha is evaluating or working with
- Know what they are trying to build internally vs. outsource
- Keep the "2-3 months vs. 8 months" delivery advantage visible — it is the
  strongest proof point we have

** Technical Architecture & Fractional CTO Responsibilities

This section covers the technical leadership mandate — distinct from the engagement
and delivery dimensions above. As Fractional CTO, the remit is to own the technology
direction for Yamaha, not to execute it day-to-day.

*** Technical Strategy & Roadmap

- Maintain a living technology roadmap for Yamaha — not just what's being built now,
  but where the platform needs to go in 6-18 months
- Current platform (Shopify + custom integrations) is a GTM vehicle, not a long-term
  architecture; own the decision of when and how to evolve beyond it
- Define the data strategy for the 10M Yamaha customer base — the platform is
  sitting on a significant data asset that is currently underutilised
- Align the technology roadmap to YMIF's investment thesis (music startups, AI in
  music) — identify where technology decisions open or close future options

*** Architecture Oversight

- Review and approve all significant architectural decisions across teams — Code
  Rapper, Data Culture, and Tarka Labs should not make major technology choices
  without your sign-off
- Ensure architectural coherence across the six separate product areas (Spotify
  integration, AI features, etc.) — fragmentation here is a long-term liability
- Maintain a set of Architecture Decision Records (ADRs) for key choices made —
  rationale, alternatives considered, trade-offs accepted
- Conduct a quarterly architecture health review: scalability, maintainability,
  integration fragility, dependency risk

*** Build vs. Buy Advisory

Every significant technology decision should go through this lens before commitment:
- *Build:* When it is core to Yamaha's competitive differentiation
- *Buy:* When a proven SaaS/API solution covers 80%+ of the need
- *Partner:* When the capability is better sourced from a specialist

Current areas requiring a clear build/buy position:
- Creator Pass payment and subscription infrastructure (beyond Shopify's defaults)
- Music metadata and rights management
- AI/ML capabilities for music recommendations or creation tools
- Analytics and data warehouse for customer insights

*** Technical Due Diligence

Regular reviews of what has been built — not to micromanage, but to catch problems
before they become client-visible crises:
- *Monthly:* Code quality spot-check across active workstreams — not a full audit,
  a targeted review of the highest-risk areas
- *Quarterly:* Full technical health review covering security posture, performance
  benchmarks, test coverage, and documentation completeness
- *On handoff:* Any work delivered by a new team or vendor gets a technical review
  before it is presented to Yamaha as done

*** Security & Compliance

Creator Pass is a consumer platform touching payment data and personal information
at scale. This cannot be treated as a delivery team concern — it is a CTO concern.

*Immediate posture to establish:*
- Payment flow: PCI DSS compliance scope — know what Shopify covers and what falls
  on the application layer
- Data privacy: GDPR and CCPA obligations for the 10M customer base — consent,
  data retention, right to deletion
- API security: authentication, rate limiting, and input validation across all
  custom integrations
- Third-party vendor risk: any SaaS tool that touches customer data needs to be
  assessed for data handling practices

*Ongoing:*
- Security is a standing agenda item in the monthly commercial review
- Any new integration or vendor must pass a lightweight security checklist before
  approval
- Incident response plan: define what happens if there is a data breach or outage

*** Vendor & Technology Evaluation

Yamaha should not commit to any significant technology vendor or tool without your
input. Establish a lightweight evaluation process:
1. What problem does this solve, and is there a better alternative?
2. What does lock-in look like, and is it acceptable?
3. What are the data handling and security practices?
4. What is the total cost of ownership over 2 years, not just the licence fee?
5. Can we exit cleanly if needed?

Maintain a vendor register: what tools are in use, what they touch, renewal dates,
and any known risks.

*** Engineering Standards

Set the quality bar across all teams working on this account:
- *Definition of Done:* A feature is not done until it is tested, documented, and
  reviewed. Agree this with all four department leads and hold to it.
- *Code review:* All production code gets reviewed before merge — no exceptions for
  deadline pressure
- *Documentation:* Every integration, API, and non-obvious architectural decision
  gets documented. The knowledge must not live only in engineers' heads.
- *Incident response:* Production incidents get a brief post-mortem (5 mins written)
  — not to assign blame, but to prevent recurrence

*** Team & Hiring Advisory

As Fractional CTO, you have a view across both Sedin's team and Yamaha's internal
capability. Use it:
- Assess whether the current team mix (Code Rapper, Data Culture, Marketing, Tarka
  Labs) has the right skills for where the platform needs to go in 12 months
- Advise Yamaha on any internal technical hires they are considering — role design,
  interview approach, what to look for
- Flag skill gaps before they become delivery risks: if no one on the team has built
  at the scale Creator Pass needs, say so early

*** Innovation Pipeline

A Fractional CTO is not just a technical guardian — they are a source of technical
opportunity. Bring one relevant technology idea per quarter that Yamaha didn't ask
for:
- AI/ML applications specific to music (recommendation, generation, rights detection)
- Data monetisation opportunities from the 10M customer base
- Emerging platforms or protocols relevant to the music industry
- Technical patterns from YMIF's portfolio companies that could benefit Creator Pass

Frame these as business opportunities first, technology solutions second.

** Proving the Model: The Replication Playbook

The meta-objective: prove that Sedin can operate as a unified technology partner at
the $1M+ level, then repeat the model for other accounts.

- Keep a running engagement log: what worked, what failed, what surprised
- After June (billing unlocked), write a one-page internal case study:
  - How we delivered
  - What the client valued most
  - What the internal coordination model looked like
  - What we'd do differently
- This becomes the *Sedin Unified Partner Playbook* — the template for the next
  Yamaha-type client

** Success Metrics

| Timeframe   | What Success Looks Like                                              |
|-------------+----------------------------------------------------------------------|
| End of June | Yamaha sees the value demo and billing unlocks                       |
| End of June | Zero client-visible coordination failures or "many teams" moments    |
| End of June | Yamaha knows your name and asks for you specifically                 |
| Q3          | At least one expansion opportunity identified and in discussion       |
| Q3          | Yamaha is not comparing us to what they could build internally        |
| Q4          | Engagement cited as proof case for Sedin unified partner model       |
| Long term   | Yamaha is a $1M+ annually renewable account                          |

** The Single Most Important Habit

Know what Yamaha is thinking *before* they say it. Proactive communication beats
reactive firefighting every time. The best client partners in the industry spend
more time thinking about the client's next problem than their own next deliverable.

One deck, one voice, one team. Bring one strategic recommendation they didn't ask
for. Review internally before sending anything to Yamaha.

** Daily Operating Rhythm

*** Morning (30 min)

| Activity                                         | Purpose                                     |
|--------------------------------------------------+---------------------------------------------|
| Scan all Yamaha threads / email                  | Nothing surprises you in client calls       |
| Attend or review dept. standups; note key points | Know blockers before they fester — =C-c c ys= |
| Identify the one thing that could go wrong today | Fix it before it becomes a client issue     |
| Check delivery tracker for overdue items         | No commitment falls through the cracks      |

*** Core Day

*Internal — keep short, keep tight:*
- Attend dept. standups; you summarise the key points (what shipped, what's next,
  any blockers) — no extra work pushed onto leads. Capture with =C-c c ys=.
- Synthesize into one coherent picture before any client interaction
- Escalate blockers before EOD, not tomorrow
- Update the risk register if anything material shifts

*External — deliberate, controlled:*
- All Yamaha communication routes through you
- If another team member communicates directly, you are CC'd and pre-approved
- Respond to Yamaha within 2 hours during business hours — speed signals confidence
- Bring one proactive observation or idea per week — don't just report status

*** End of Day (15 min)

- Update the delivery tracker
- Flag any Yamaha ask without an assigned owner
- Send a proactive note to Yamaha if something meaningful shipped — don't wait for
  the weekly call

** Weekly Rhythm

| Day       | Activities                                                                               |
|-----------+------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Monday    | 1. Internal sync with all dept. leads — commitments vs. reality gap. (=C-c c yi=)        |
|           | 2. Update risk register — new risks? mitigations to action? (=C-c c yr=)                 |
| Tuesday   | Account growth review — any expansion opportunity to surface this week?                  |
| Wednesday | Written status update to Yamaha (3-5 bullets: shipped, next, decisions needed from them) |
| Thursday  | Architecture & technical review — decisions made this week, anything to challenge?       |
|           | Review stakeholder map — any new contacts, any relationship that needs warming?          |
| Friday    | 1. Yamaha call or async Loom — you present, one voice. (=C-c c ym=)                      |
|           | 2. Internal retro — what comms went sideways, what coordination failed, fix it           |

** Monthly and Quarterly Rhythms

These cadences are standard in engagement director and client partner roles and are
typically absent from informal consulting arrangements. They are what separates a
vendor relationship from a strategic partnership.

*** Monthly: Client Health Check
- Send Yamaha a brief satisfaction pulse — 3 questions max, async format
- Qualitative: what's working, what would they change, what would they love to see
- Review internally and identify one thing to improve and one to double down on
- Do not wait for problems to surface organically

*** Monthly: Commercial Review
- Track billable time vs. SOW commitments
- Flag scope creep within 48 hours of identifying it — bring it to Yamaha as an
  opportunity, not a dispute: "here's what we can add and what it would take"
- Ensure invoices are sent on time and match the SOW exactly — late or inaccurate
  invoices erode trust faster than delivery misses
- Identify any expansion of work that should be covered by a new or amended SOW

*** Quarterly: Executive Business Review (QBR)
- 60-90 minute structured session with Yamaha senior stakeholders
- Cover: what we delivered, business impact achieved, what's next, roadmap alignment
- Bring one strategic recommendation they didn't ask for — this is the "trusted
  advisor" signal
- Document outcomes and send a written summary within 24 hours of the call
- Use QBR to surface the renewal or expansion conversation naturally

** Communication Framework

*** The Cardinal Rule

Yamaha should never see the seams between Sedin departments.

- One Slack channel or email thread with Yamaha, owned by you
- Departments do not CC Yamaha on inter-team coordination
- Disagreements are resolved internally before Yamaha hears anything
- All commitments to Yamaha are made by you — only you commit timelines and scope

*** The "One Team" Narrative

In every Yamaha touchpoint:
- Use "we" — not "our Tarka Labs team" or "our data team"
- Reference capabilities, not org structure: "we have deep expertise in X"
- Prepare a one-paragraph team introduction for any new Yamaha stakeholder that
  frames the team as a single integrated unit

*** Escalation Protocol

If a department will miss a commitment:
1. You find out as early as possible (the daily standup habit is what enables this)
2. You tell Yamaha *before* the deadline, *not after*, with a revised plan in hand
3. You own the message — never "our marketing team dropped the ball"

Log any commitment (made or received) immediately with =C-c c yc=.

*** Communication Templates to Build

- [ ] Weekly status update (consistent format, 3-5 bullets, takes 10 min to write)
- [ ] Escalation notice (acknowledge, explain, revised plan — no blame)
- [ ] New stakeholder introduction (one paragraph, one-team narrative)
- [ ] Meeting follow-up / action items (sent within 2 hours of any call)
- [ ] Scope change framing (opportunity framing, not dispute framing)

** Internal Coordination Model

*** Department Lead Relationships

Treat each lead as your delivery partner for their domain. Establish with each:
- Weekly 30-min 1:1
- A shared tracker they update (not a meeting — a doc)
- Clear ownership split: they own *how*, you own *what and when* with the client

The four leads to align:
1. Code Rapper — development / technical delivery
2. Data Culture — data, analytics, insights workstream
3. Marketing — brand, content, client-facing materials
4. Tarka Labs — engineering / product leadership

*** Yamaha Engagement Overview (Internal Brief)

A single document every team member reads before touching this account:
- What we've committed to and by when
- Who owns each workstream by department
- Yamaha's success criteria (in their words, not ours)
- Key contacts at Yamaha: names, roles, what success looks like to each of them
- What we must *not* say or surface externally: internal tensions, org structure,
  billing disputes, staffing issues, cross-department friction

Every new person touching this engagement reads this brief before their first
client email or call.

*** New Team Member Onboarding Protocol

Standard practice in enterprise consulting; typically missing in agency engagements.
- *Brief:* Read the Yamaha Engagement Overview before first client contact
- *Shadow:* Sit in on at least one client call before speaking in one
- *Introduction:* You introduce them to Yamaha, with context on their role and
  what capability they bring to the team

*** Preventing the "Many Vendors" Problem

- One slide deck template for all Yamaha presentations
- One tone of voice: professional, capable, collaborative, commercially aware
- One project board / tracker that all teams update — Yamaha can have read access
- No department-specific branding in client deliverables

** Delivery Management

*** Delivery Tracker

A living document updated daily, reviewed weekly. Add new entries with =C-c c yc=.

| Commitment            | Made On | Promised By | Owner (internal) | Status      | Yamaha Notified? |
|-----------------------+---------+-------------+------------------+-------------+------------------|
| Creator Pass checkout | May 12  | May 19      | Tarka Labs       | Done        | Yes              |
| [next item]           |         |             |                  | In Progress |                  |

Any row where "Owner" is blank is a fire. Any row where "Yamaha Notified?" is No
and Status is Done is a missed opportunity.

*** Risk Register

Standard in Engagement Director and Program Director roles; typically absent from
informal consulting arrangements. Review in Monday's internal sync. Log new risks
as they surface with =C-c c yr=.

| Risk                              | Likelihood | Impact | Mitigation                                   | Owner       |
|-----------------------------------+------------+--------+----------------------------------------------+-------------|
| Internal coordination breakdown   | High       | High   | Daily async standup, weekly sync, you as hub  | You         |
| Scope creep without billing       | Medium     | High   | SOW review monthly, 48hr escalation rule      | You         |
| Key person dependency at Yamaha   | Medium     | Medium | Build relationships with 2+ contacts          | You         |
| Delivery miss at end of June      | Medium     | High   | Weekly tracker, buffer built into estimates   | Dept. leads |
| Yamaha loses confidence in unity  | Low        | High   | Consistent comms discipline, one-voice rule   | You         |
| New stakeholder without briefing  | Low        | Medium | Onboarding protocol, read brief before call   | You         |

*** Scope and Commercial Management

- Maintain an active log of scope changes and decisions
- Flag any out-of-scope work within 48 hours of identifying it
- Frame additions as opportunities: "here's what we can add and what it would take"
- Review SOW monthly — know exactly what is and isn't covered
- Ensure invoices are sent on time and reconcile against the delivery tracker

** Account Growth and Strategy

This is a forward-looking dimension standard in Client Partner roles. It distinguishes
a vendor (delivers what's asked) from a strategic partner (shapes what gets asked).

*** Know Their Roadmap

- Understand what YMIF is building for the next 12 months beyond Creator Pass
- Identify where Sedin could play before Yamaha has to ask
- Bring one strategic recommendation per quarter that they didn't ask for

*** Expansion Opportunities Within the Account

#+begin_example
Creator Pass v2        — Features beyond the current Shopify build
Data & Analytics       — 10M customer base is an asset; what can be done with it?
AI/ML in Music         — Adjacent to the YMIF portfolio investment thesis
Other Portfolio Cos    — YMIF invests in startups; other portfolio companies may
                         need the same technology partnership
#+end_example

*** Business Context: Know Their Business, Not Just the Project

Standard at Accenture/ThoughtWorks: every person on a client engagement should
be able to answer:
- What business outcome does Creator Pass ultimately serve for Yamaha?
- What would make this project fail, and have we named that risk explicitly?
- What would we recommend if we were Yamaha's CTO?

Embed this in every project kickoff: 30 min on client business context, not just
technical context.

*** Competitive Awareness

- Know who else Yamaha is evaluating or working with
- Know what they are trying to build internally vs. outsource
- Keep the "2-3 months vs. 8 months" delivery advantage visible — it is the
  strongest proof point we have

** Technical Architecture & Fractional CTO Responsibilities

This section covers the technical leadership mandate — distinct from the engagement
and delivery dimensions above. As Fractional CTO, the remit is to own the technology
direction for Yamaha, not to execute it day-to-day.

*** Technical Strategy & Roadmap

- Maintain a living technology roadmap for Yamaha — not just what's being built now,
  but where the platform needs to go in 6-18 months
- Current platform (Shopify + custom integrations) is a GTM vehicle, not a long-term
  architecture; own the decision of when and how to evolve beyond it
- Define the data strategy for the 10M Yamaha customer base — the platform is
  sitting on a significant data asset that is currently underutilised
- Align the technology roadmap to YMIF's investment thesis (music startups, AI in
  music) — identify where technology decisions open or close future options

*** Architecture Oversight

- Review and approve all significant architectural decisions across teams — Code
  Rapper, Data Culture, and Tarka Labs should not make major technology choices
  without your sign-off
- Ensure architectural coherence across the six separate product areas (Spotify
  integration, AI features, etc.) — fragmentation here is a long-term liability
- Maintain a set of Architecture Decision Records (ADRs) for key choices made —
  rationale, alternatives considered, trade-offs accepted
- Conduct a quarterly architecture health review: scalability, maintainability,
  integration fragility, dependency risk

*** Build vs. Buy Advisory

Every significant technology decision should go through this lens before commitment:
- *Build:* When it is core to Yamaha's competitive differentiation
- *Buy:* When a proven SaaS/API solution covers 80%+ of the need
- *Partner:* When the capability is better sourced from a specialist

Current areas requiring a clear build/buy position:
- Creator Pass payment and subscription infrastructure (beyond Shopify's defaults)
- Music metadata and rights management
- AI/ML capabilities for music recommendations or creation tools
- Analytics and data warehouse for customer insights

*** Technical Due Diligence

Regular reviews of what has been built — not to micromanage, but to catch problems
before they become client-visible crises:
- *Monthly:* Code quality spot-check across active workstreams — not a full audit,
  a targeted review of the highest-risk areas
- *Quarterly:* Full technical health review covering security posture, performance
  benchmarks, test coverage, and documentation completeness
- *On handoff:* Any work delivered by a new team or vendor gets a technical review
  before it is presented to Yamaha as done

*** Security & Compliance

Creator Pass is a consumer platform touching payment data and personal information
at scale. This cannot be treated as a delivery team concern — it is a CTO concern.

*Immediate posture to establish:*
- Payment flow: PCI DSS compliance scope — know what Shopify covers and what falls
  on the application layer
- Data privacy: GDPR and CCPA obligations for the 10M customer base — consent,
  data retention, right to deletion
- API security: authentication, rate limiting, and input validation across all
  custom integrations
- Third-party vendor risk: any SaaS tool that touches customer data needs to be
  assessed for data handling practices

*Ongoing:*
- Security is a standing agenda item in the monthly commercial review
- Any new integration or vendor must pass a lightweight security checklist before
  approval
- Incident response plan: define what happens if there is a data breach or outage

*** Vendor & Technology Evaluation

Yamaha should not commit to any significant technology vendor or tool without your
input. Establish a lightweight evaluation process:
1. What problem does this solve, and is there a better alternative?
2. What does lock-in look like, and is it acceptable?
3. What are the data handling and security practices?
4. What is the total cost of ownership over 2 years, not just the licence fee?
5. Can we exit cleanly if needed?

Maintain a vendor register: what tools are in use, what they touch, renewal dates,
and any known risks.

*** Engineering Standards

Set the quality bar across all teams working on this account:
- *Definition of Done:* A feature is not done until it is tested, documented, and
  reviewed. Agree this with all four department leads and hold to it.
- *Code review:* All production code gets reviewed before merge — no exceptions for
  deadline pressure
- *Documentation:* Every integration, API, and non-obvious architectural decision
  gets documented. The knowledge must not live only in engineers' heads.
- *Incident response:* Production incidents get a brief post-mortem (5 mins written)
  — not to assign blame, but to prevent recurrence

*** Team & Hiring Advisory

As Fractional CTO, you have a view across both Sedin's team and Yamaha's internal
capability. Use it:
- Assess whether the current team mix (Code Rapper, Data Culture, Marketing, Tarka
  Labs) has the right skills for where the platform needs to go in 12 months
- Advise Yamaha on any internal technical hires they are considering — role design,
  interview approach, what to look for
- Flag skill gaps before they become delivery risks: if no one on the team has built
  at the scale Creator Pass needs, say so early

*** Innovation Pipeline

A Fractional CTO is not just a technical guardian — they are a source of technical
opportunity. Bring one relevant technology idea per quarter that Yamaha didn't ask
for:
- AI/ML applications specific to music (recommendation, generation, rights detection)
- Data monetisation opportunities from the 10M customer base
- Emerging platforms or protocols relevant to the music industry
- Technical patterns from YMIF's portfolio companies that could benefit Creator Pass

Frame these as business opportunities first, technology solutions second.

** Proving the Model: The Replication Playbook

The meta-objective: prove that Sedin can operate as a unified technology partner at
the $1M+ level, then repeat the model for other accounts.

- Keep a running engagement log: what worked, what failed, what surprised
- After June (billing unlocked), write a one-page internal case study:
  - How we delivered
  - What the client valued most
  - What the internal coordination model looked like
  - What we'd do differently
- This becomes the *Sedin Unified Partner Playbook* — the template for the next
  Yamaha-type client

** Success Metrics

| Timeframe   | What Success Looks Like                                              |
|-------------+----------------------------------------------------------------------|
| End of June | Yamaha sees the value demo and billing unlocks                       |
| End of June | Zero client-visible coordination failures or "many teams" moments    |
| End of June | Yamaha knows your name and asks for you specifically                 |
| Q3          | At least one expansion opportunity identified and in discussion       |
| Q3          | Yamaha is not comparing us to what they could build internally        |
| Q4          | Engagement cited as proof case for Sedin unified partner model       |
| Long term   | Yamaha is a $1M+ annually renewable account                          |

** The Single Most Important Habit

Know what Yamaha is thinking *before* they say it. Proactive communication beats
reactive firefighting every time. The best client partners in the industry spend
more time thinking about the client's next problem than their own next deliverable.

  (defun bh/is-project-p ()
    "Any task with a todo keyword subtask"
    (save-restriction
      (widen)
      (let ((has-subtask)
            (subtree-end (save-excursion (org-end-of-subtree t)))
            (is-a-task (member (nth 2 (org-heading-components)) org-todo-keywords-1)))
        (save-excursion
          (forward-line 1)
          (while (and (not has-subtask)
                      (< (point) subtree-end)
                      (re-search-forward "^\*+ " subtree-end t))
            (when (member (org-get-todo-state) org-todo-keywords-1)
              (setq has-subtask t))))
        (and is-a-task has-subtask))))

  (defun bh/is-project-subtree-p ()
    "Any task with a todo keyword that is in a project subtree.
               Callers of this function already widen the buffer view."
    (let ((task (save-excursion (org-back-to-heading 'invisible-ok)
                                (point))))
      (save-excursion
        (bh/find-project-task)
        (if (equal (point) task)
            nil
          t))))

  (defun bh/is-task-p ()
    "Any task with a todo keyword and no subtask"
    (save-restriction
      (widen)
      (let ((has-subtask)
            (subtree-end (save-excursion (org-end-of-subtree t)))
            (is-a-task (member (nth 2 (org-heading-components)) org-todo-keywords-1)))
        (save-excursion
          (forward-line 1)
          (while (and (not has-subtask)
                      (< (point) subtree-end)
                      (re-search-forward "^\*+ " subtree-end t))
            (when (member (org-get-todo-state) org-todo-keywords-1)
              (setq has-subtask t))))
        (and is-a-task (not has-subtask)))))

  (defun bh/is-subproject-p ()
    "Any task which is a subtask of another project"
    (let ((is-subproject)
          (is-a-task (member (nth 2 (org-heading-components)) org-todo-keywords-1)))
      (save-excursion
        (while (and (not is-subproject) (org-up-heading-safe))
          (when (member (nth 2 (org-heading-components)) org-todo-keywords-1)
            (setq is-subproject t))))
      (and is-a-task is-subproject)))

  (defun bh/skip-stuck-projects ()
    "Skip trees that are not stuck projects"
    (save-restriction
      (widen)
      (let ((next-headline (save-excursion (or (outline-next-heading) (point-max)))))
        (if (bh/is-project-p)
            (let* ((subtree-end (save-excursion (org-end-of-subtree t)))
                   (has-next ))
              (save-excursion
                (forward-line 1)
                (while (and (not has-next) (< (point) subtree-end) (re-search-forward "^\\*+ NEXT " subtree-end t))
                  (unless (member "WAITING" (org-get-tags-at))
                    (setq has-next t))))
              (if has-next
                  nil
                next-headline)) ; a stuck project, has subtasks but no next task
          nil))))

  (defun bh/agenda-sort (a b)
    "Sorting strategy for agenda items.
               Late deadlines first, then scheduled, then non-late deadlines"
    (let (result num-a num-b)
      (cond
					; time specific items are already sorted first by org-agenda-sorting-strategy

					; non-deadline and non-scheduled items next
       ((bh/agenda-sort-test 'bh/is-not-scheduled-or-deadline a b))

					; deadlines for today next
       ((bh/agenda-sort-test 'bh/is-due-deadline a b))

					; late deadlines next
       ((bh/agenda-sort-test-num 'bh/is-late-deadline '> a b))

					; scheduled items for today next
       ((bh/agenda-sort-test 'bh/is-scheduled-today a b))

					; late scheduled items next
       ((bh/agenda-sort-test-num 'bh/is-scheduled-late '> a b))

					; pending deadlines last
       ((bh/agenda-sort-test-num 'bh/is-pending-deadline '< a b))

					; finally default to unsorted
       (t (setq result nil)))
      result))

  (defmacro bh/agenda-sort-test (fn a b)
    "Test for agenda sort"
    `(cond
					; if both match leave them unsorted
      ((and (apply ,fn (list ,a))
            (apply ,fn (list ,b)))
       (setq result nil))
					; if a matches put a first
      ((apply ,fn (list ,a))
       (setq result -1))
					; otherwise if b matches put b first
      ((apply ,fn (list ,b))
       (setq result 1))
					; if none match leave them unsorted
      (t nil)))

  (defmacro bh/agenda-sort-test-num (fn compfn a b)
    `(cond
      ((apply ,fn (list ,a))
       (setq num-a (string-to-number (match-string 1 ,a)))
       (if (apply ,fn (list ,b))
           (progn
             (setq num-b (string-to-number (match-string 1 ,b)))
             (setq result (if (apply ,compfn (list num-a num-b))
                              -1
                            1)))
         (setq result -1)))
      ((apply ,fn (list ,b))
       (setq result 1))
      (t nil)))

  (defun bh/is-not-scheduled-or-deadline (date-str)

  (defun bh/is-late-deadline (date-str)

  (defun bh/is-pending-deadline (date-str)

  (defun bh/is-deadline (date-str)

        (bh/is-late-deadline date-str)
        (bh/is-pending-deadline date-str)))

    (or (bh/is-scheduled-today date-str)
        (bh/is-scheduled-late date-str)))

      ;; for mac, use org-show-notification, which is more limited
      (setq appt-disp-window-function
	    (lambda (remaining new-time msg)
	      (org-show-notification msg)))

    ;; for other systems, use notifications-notify
    (setq appt-disp-window-function

	    (notifications-notify
	     :title (format "In %s minutes" remaining)

  (defun bh/view-next-project ()
    (interactive)
    (let (num-project-left current-project)
      (unless (marker-position org-agenda-restrict-begin)
        (goto-char (point-min))
					; Clear all of the existing markers on the list
        (while bh/project-list
          (set-marker (pop bh/project-list) nil))
        (re-search-forward "Tasks to Refile")
        (forward-visible-line 1))

					; Build a new project marker list
      (unless bh/project-list
        (while (< (point) (point-max))
          (while (and (< (point) (point-max))
                      (or (not (org-get-at-bol 'org-hd-marker))
                          (org-with-point-at (org-get-at-bol 'org-hd-marker)
                            (or (not (bh/is-project-p))
                                (bh/is-project-subtree-p)))))
            (forward-visible-line 1))
          (when (< (point) (point-max))
            (add-to-list 'bh/project-list (copy-marker (org-get-at-bol 'org-hd-marker)) 'append))
          (forward-visible-line 1)))

					; Pop off the first marker on the list and display
      (setq current-project (pop bh/project-list))
      (when current-project
        (org-with-point-at current-project
          (setq bh/hide-scheduled-and-waiting-next-tasks nil)
          (bh/narrow-to-project))
					; Remove the marker
        (setq current-project nil)
        (org-agenda-redo)
        (beginning-of-buffer)
        (setq num-projects-left (length bh/project-list))
        (if (> num-projects-left 0)
            (message "%s projects left to view" num-projects-left)
          (beginning-of-buffer)
          (setq bh/hide-scheduled-and-waiting-next-tasks t)
          (error "All projects viewed.")))))

    "Visit each parent task and change NEXT states to TODO"
